--- title: "Data Structures: Vectors" author: "Enrico Toffalini" include-in-header: ../assets/slidesheader.html format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false css: custom.css theme: default slide-number: c/t self-contained: true code-fold: false code-summary: "Show code" code-overflow: wrap title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: "figures/psicostatLogo.png" data-background-size: "contain" data-background-opacity: "0.15" execute: echo: true output: true --- ## Data Structures
- Most often you don't work with single scalar variables (e.g., `age = 20`), but with more complex data structures like **vectors**, **matrices**, **dataframes**, **lists**, that allow you to **organize and store complex information** - Many **functions** are created for handling such structures (e.g., `lm()` takes vectors or dataframes as input) - When you *process data*, *fit models*, *plot outputs*, you generally work with these data structures
## Vectors Simple one-dimensional structures that store elements of a single type
Here is an actual **example** (of a *numerical* vector):
## Vectors as 1-D Arrays Vectors are just special cases of **arrays**
## Create Vectors with `c()` Vectors can easily be **created using the `c()`** base function, with a sequence of elements separated by *commas* "**`,`**" Vectors can be of different types. The following example shows a *character* vector (note the *quotes* **`" "`** around objects):
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Teachers = c("Pastore", "Kiesner", "Granziol", "Toffalini", "Calignano", "Epifania", "Bastianelli", "Altoe") ``` ::: or numeric: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, 5, 15, 5) ``` :::
## Vectors Must be Homogeneous Vectors must contain elements of the **same type**. If you mix types, R will automatically **coerce** the elements to a single type, which may lead to undesired results. Therefore, **avoid mixing data types!** Example:
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, "tbd", 15, 5) Hours ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "10" "15" "20" "10" "15" "tbd" "15" "5" ``` ::: ::: everything was coerced to become a character! If needed, use **`NA`** (Not Available): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, NA, 15, 5) Hours # remains a numerical vector, NA does not affect type ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 15 20 10 15 NA 15 5 ``` ::: :::
## Vectors Must be Homogeneous You may **coerce a vector** to be a particular type if needed ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, "tbd", 15, 5) Hours ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "10" "15" "20" "10" "15" "tbd" "15" "5" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.numeric(Hours) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: NAs introduced by coercion ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 15 20 10 15 NA 15 5 ``` ::: ::: *But be careful!* Elements that cannot be coerced to the target type will be replaced with NA ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c("10", "15,", "20", " 10", "15 ", "tbd", "15.", "5_") as.numeric(Hours) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: NAs introduced by coercion ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 NA 20 10 15 NA 15 NA ``` ::: ::: ## ### NA and NULL in vectors Recall the special values and objects introduced with basic data types: **`NA`** occupies a position in a vector; **`NULL`** contributes no element. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(NA) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(1, NULL, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 3 ``` ::: ::: Use `is.na()` to identify missing values in a vector. ## Indexing Vectors Select/extract elements with **INDEXING** using square brackets **`[]`**:
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, 5, 15, 5) Hours[4] # a single element ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} Hours[5:7] # a range of elements ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15 5 15 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} Hours[c(1,3,6)] # specific elements ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 20 5 ``` ::: ::: Know the **length** of a vector using the `length()` function, and use it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(Hours) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours[length(Hours)] # use it to extract the last element ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: :::
## Indexing Vectors **Negative indexing** You can use the *minus* sign **`-`** to select **all elements except some** from a vector. (This method is also applicable to dataframes)
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, 5, 15, 5) Hours[-4] # ALL BUT a single element ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 15 20 15 5 15 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} Hours[-c(5:7)] # ALL BUT a range of elements ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 15 20 10 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} Hours[-c(1,3,6)] # ALL BUT specific elements ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15 10 15 15 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} Hours[-length(Hours)] # ALL BUT the last element ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10 15 20 10 15 5 15 ``` ::: :::
## Logical Indexing Often, you'll need to extract values from a vector based on specific *logical* conditions. Here's an example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, 5, 15, 5) Hours[Hours >= 15] # extract only values greater than or equal to 15 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15 20 15 15 ``` ::: ::: This is called *logical indexing* because you are selecting elements based on a logical vector (i.e., a sequence of `TRUE`, `FALSE`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours >= 15 # the logical vector actually inside the square brackets ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: Also, you can use a vector to extract values **from another vector**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Teachers[Hours >= 15] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Kiesner" "Granziol" "Calignano" "Bastianelli" ``` ::: ::: ## Indexing and Assignment With indexing, you can not only select, but also **assign or modify** elements in a vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, 5, 15, 5) Hours[1] = 0 # assign a new value Hours[3] = Hours[3]+50 # modify an existing element Hours ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 15 70 10 15 5 15 5 ``` ::: ::: You can even assign values **outside the current range** of the vector. But what happens? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours[20] = 5 Hours ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 15 70 10 15 5 15 5 NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA 5 ``` ::: ::: ## Operating on Vectors You can simultaneously apply an operation to a whole vector, like: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, 5, 15, 5) Hours / 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 4 2 3 1 3 1 ``` ::: ::: Of course, this is useful when you want to save the result as a new vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ECTS = Hours / 5 ``` ::: Similarly, you can apply functions to all elements of a vector: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sqrt(Hours) # computes square root of each element ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.162278 3.872983 4.472136 3.162278 3.872983 2.236068 3.872983 2.236068 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} log(Hours) # computes the natural logarithm of each element ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.302585 2.708050 2.995732 2.302585 2.708050 1.609438 2.708050 1.609438 ``` ::: ::: ## Summary Statistics on Vectors A whole vector may serve to compute summary statistics, for example using functions such as **`mean()`, `sd()`, `median()`, `quantile()`, `max()`, `min()`**:
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(Hours) # returns the average value (mean) of the vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11.875 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sd(Hours) # returns the Standard Deviation of the vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.303301 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} median(Hours) # returns the median value of the vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12.5 ``` ::: :::
## Summary Statistics on Vectors A whole vector may serve to compute summary statistics, for example using functions such as **`mean()`, `sd()`, `median()`, `quantile()`, `max()`, `min()`**:
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} quantile(Hours, probs=c(.25, .50, .75)) # returns desired quantiles ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 25% 50% 75% 8.75 12.50 15.00 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} max(Hours) # returns largest value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 20 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} min(Hours) # returns smallest value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(Hours) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2.1.DataStruc-1_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=432} ::: :::
A quick base R plot lets us *see* the distribution. Figure design belongs to the ggplot2 course. ## ### Summary Statistics - Managing Missing (`NA`) Values All of the previous summary statistics will **fail** if there is even a single `NA` value: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, NA, 15, 5) mean(Hours) # a single NA value implies that the average is impossible to determine ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} quantile(Hours, probs=c(.25, .75)) # quantile() will even return an Error ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in quantile.default(Hours, probs = c(0.25, 0.75)): missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE ``` ::: ::: You can easily manage missing values by adding the **`na.rm=TRUE`** argument: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(Hours, na.rm=TRUE) # NA values are ignored ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12.85714 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} quantile(Hours, probs=c(.25, .75), na.rm=TRUE) # NA values are ignored ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 25% 75% 10 15 ``` ::: ::: ## ### Replacing `NA` With the Average Value
Replacing a missing value with the average across valid values is risky, as it may alter many other summary statistics, but it is a good example for understanding different concepts seen so far: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Hours = c(10, 15, 20, 10, 15, NA, 15, 5) # compute the average value ignoring NAs, and put it wherever # there is an NA value in the vector Hours[is.na(Hours)] = mean(Hours, na.rm=TRUE) # now let's inspect the updated content of the vector Hours ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.00000 15.00000 20.00000 10.00000 15.00000 12.85714 15.00000 5.00000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # by the way... na.rm=TRUE is no longer needed now, as NA is no longer there mean(Hours) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12.85714 ``` ::: :::
## Frequency Counts Another useful summary statistic is the **frequency count**, which shows how often each unique value appears in a vector. You can use the **`table()`** function to calculate frequencies easily: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} type = c("METHODOLOGY", "METHODOLOGY", "PROGRAMMING", "SOFT SKILLS", "SOFT SKILLS", "METHODOLOGY", "SOFT SKILLS", "METHODOLOGY", "PROGRAMMING") table(type) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` type METHODOLOGY PROGRAMMING SOFT SKILLS 4 2 3 ``` ::: ::: *Be careful:* R is case-sensitive! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} type = c("METHODOLOGY", "methodology", "PROGRAMMING", "SOFT SKILLS", "SOFT SKILLS", "METHODOLOGY", "SOFT SKILLS", "METHODOLOGY", "Programming") table(type) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` type methodology METHODOLOGY Programming PROGRAMMING SOFT SKILLS 1 3 1 1 3 ``` ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
